steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a generalized shuffle framework for privacy amplification in shuffle-model differential privacy: background on the shuffle model, the gap in existing amplification analyses, and our two main contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Background: shuffle model of differential privacy and its privacy amplification
- Gap: existing analyses assume uniform, limited local privacy parameters
- Contribution 1: GSPA framework and new amplification analysis
- Contribution 2: applying GSPA to analysis tasks, with findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - shuffle model: state-of-the-art for balancing privacy and utility in DP data analysis
  - traditional DP: trusted server (aggregator) collects all users' data first
  - not feasible/practical when no trusted curator exists
  - LDP: users add noise individually -> low utility from accumulated noise
  - shuffle DP: shuffler between users and server, randomly shuffles noisy data before sending to server
  - privacy amplification: small local noise -> strong guarantee against untrusted server
  - many studies on proving better (tighter) amplification
- Gap
  - most work: (\epsilon_{0},\delta_{0}) -LDP randomizer, uniform and limited local parameters
  - e.g. one work assumes 0<\epsilon_{0}<1/2 and \delta_{0}=0
  - recent work: bound for personalized \epsilon_{i} per user i (fixed \delta_{0}) -- rough, room to improve
- Contribution 1: GSPA
  - Generalized Shuffle framework for Privacy Amplification (GSPA)
  - arbitrary local privacy parameters, new amplification analysis
  - technique: Functional Differential Privacy + distance between two multinomial distributions (Theorem 1 and 2)
  - uniform and personalized settings: lower privacy bounds exceed existing results (Figure 2)
- Contribution 2: applications
  - personalized settings on private mean, private frequency estimation, DP-SGD
  - mean/frequency (Figure 3): more conservative users -> less utility, negative linear relationship
  - conservative users' privacy parameters increase -> utility positive linear relationship
  - DP-SGD (Figure 4): constant scenario (\epsilon_{0}=0.5) stronger protection but higher test accuracy (94.8%) than U(0.01,2) scenarios (93.5%) with varying parameters

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The shuffle model is a state-of-the-art technique for balancing privacy and utility in differentially private data analysis. In traditional differential privacy, it is often assumed that there is a trusted server (or aggregator) which collects all the users' data before doing the privacy-preserving data analysis. But this may not be feasible or practical when there is no trusted curator. Because of this, Local Differential Privacy (LDP) was proposed, where differential privacy is achieved by letting the users add noises individually; however, LDP has low utility because of the accumulated noise. To solve this, the shuffle model of differential privacy (shuffle DP) puts a shuffler between the users and the server, and the shuffler randomly shuffles the noisy data before sending it to the server. Shuffle DP has an interesting theoretical privacy amplification effect, which means that a small amount of local noise can give a strong privacy guarantee against the untrusted server. Many studies have worked on proving a better (tighter) privacy amplification in shuffle DP.

However, most of the existing studies focus on the shuffle model based on an (\epsilon_{0},\delta_{0}) -LDP randomizer, where the settings of the local privacy parameters \epsilon_{0} and \delta_{0} are uniform and limited. For example, one prior work assumes 0<\epsilon_{0}<1/2 and \delta_{0}=0. A recent work gives a privacy bound for a local personalized privacy parameter \epsilon_{i} for each user i (with a fixed \delta_{0}), but the bound is rather rough and there is a lot of room to improve it. To address this problem, we make the following contributions.

- Contribution 1: GSPA
  - Generalized Shuffle framework for Privacy Amplification (GSPA)
  - arbitrary local privacy parameters, new amplification analysis
  - technique: Functional Differential Privacy + distance between two multinomial distributions (Theorem 1 and 2)
  - uniform and personalized settings: lower privacy bounds exceed existing results (Figure 2)
- Contribution 2: applications
  - personalized settings on private mean, private frequency estimation, DP-SGD
  - mean/frequency (Figure 3): more conservative users -> less utility, negative linear relationship
  - conservative users' privacy parameters increase -> utility positive linear relationship
  - DP-SGD (Figure 4): constant scenario (\epsilon_{0}=0.5) stronger protection but higher test accuracy (94.8%) than U(0.01,2) scenarios (93.5%) with varying parameters

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The shuffle model is a state-of-the-art technique for balancing privacy and utility in differentially private data analysis. In traditional differential privacy, it is often assumed that there is a trusted server (or aggregator) which collects all the users' data before doing the privacy-preserving data analysis. But this may not be feasible or practical when there is no trusted curator. Because of this, Local Differential Privacy (LDP) was proposed, where differential privacy is achieved by letting the users add noises individually; however, LDP has low utility because of the accumulated noise. To solve this, the shuffle model of differential privacy (shuffle DP) puts a shuffler between the users and the server, and the shuffler randomly shuffles the noisy data before sending it to the server. Shuffle DP has an interesting theoretical privacy amplification effect, which means that a small amount of local noise can give a strong privacy guarantee against the untrusted server. Many studies have worked on proving a better (tighter) privacy amplification in shuffle DP.

However, most of the existing studies focus on the shuffle model based on an (\epsilon_{0},\delta_{0}) -LDP randomizer, where the settings of the local privacy parameters \epsilon_{0} and \delta_{0} are uniform and limited. For example, one prior work assumes 0<\epsilon_{0}<1/2 and \delta_{0}=0. A recent work gives a privacy bound for a local personalized privacy parameter \epsilon_{i} for each user i (with a fixed \delta_{0}), but the bound is rather rough and there is a lot of room to improve it. To address this problem, we make the following contributions.

First, we propose a Generalized Shuffle framework for Privacy Amplification (GSPA) which allows arbitrary local privacy parameters, and we give a new privacy amplification analysis. Our analysis technique uses Functional Differential Privacy and a careful analysis of the distance between two multinomial distributions (see Theorem 1 and 2). For both the uniform and the personalized privacy parameter settings, we give lower privacy bounds that exceed the existing results (see Figure 2).

Second, we apply GSPA with different personalized privacy parameter settings to different privacy-preserving analysis tasks, which include private mean, private frequency estimation and DP-SGD, to show that our approach is effective. For mean and frequency estimation with GSPA (see Figure 3), when there are more conservative users there is less utility, so there is a negative linear relationship. At the same time, when the privacy parameters of conservative users increase, the utility shows a positive linear relationship. For DP-SGD with GSPA (see Figure 4), there is an interesting phenomenon: the constant scenario (\epsilon_{0}=0.5) gives stronger privacy protection, but its test accuracy (94.8%) is higher than the accuracy (93.5%) of the U(0.01,2) scenarios, which have varying local privacy parameters.

steps.name: cited_draft
steps.text:
The shuffle model [1] is a state-of-the-art technique for balancing privacy and utility in differentially private data analysis. In traditional differential privacy, it is often assumed that there is a trusted server (or aggregator) which collects all the users' data before doing the privacy-preserving data analysis [2]. But this may not be feasible or practical when there is no trusted curator. Because of this, Local Differential Privacy (LDP) [3] was proposed, where differential privacy is achieved by letting the users add noises individually; however, LDP has low utility because of the accumulated noise. To solve this, the shuffle model of differential privacy (shuffle DP) [1,4,5] puts a shuffler between the users and the server, and the shuffler randomly shuffles the noisy data before sending it to the server. Shuffle DP has an interesting theoretical privacy amplification effect, which means that a small amount of local noise can give a strong privacy guarantee against the untrusted server. Many studies [4,5,6,7,8,9] have worked on proving a better (tighter) privacy amplification in shuffle DP.

However, most of the existing studies focus on the shuffle model based on an (\epsilon_{0},\delta_{0}) -LDP randomizer, where the settings of the local privacy parameters \epsilon_{0} and \delta_{0} are uniform and limited. For example, one prior work [5] assumes 0<\epsilon_{0}<1/2 and \delta_{0}=0. A recent work [10] gives a privacy bound for a local personalized privacy parameter \epsilon_{i} for each user i (with a fixed \delta_{0}), but the bound is rather rough and there is a lot of room to improve it. To address this problem, we make the following contributions.

First, we propose a Generalized Shuffle framework for Privacy Amplification (GSPA) which allows arbitrary local privacy parameters, and we give a new privacy amplification analysis. Our analysis technique uses Functional Differential Privacy [11] and a careful analysis of the distance between two multinomial distributions (see Theorem 1 and 2). For both the uniform and the personalized privacy parameter settings, we give lower privacy bounds that exceed the existing results (see Figure 2).

Second, we apply GSPA with different personalized privacy parameter settings to different privacy-preserving analysis tasks, which include private mean, private frequency estimation and DP-SGD, to show that our approach is effective. For mean and frequency estimation with GSPA (see Figure 3), when there are more conservative users there is less utility, so there is a negative linear relationship. At the same time, when the privacy parameters of conservative users increase, the utility shows a positive linear relationship. For DP-SGD with GSPA (see Figure 4), there is an interesting phenomenon: the constant scenario (\epsilon_{0}=0.5) gives stronger privacy protection, but its test accuracy (94.8%) is higher than the accuracy (93.5%) of the U(0.01,2) scenarios, which have varying local privacy parameters.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The shuffle model [1] is a state-of-the-art technique for balancing privacy and utility in differentially private data analysis. In traditional differential privacy, a trusted server (or aggregator) is often assumed to collect all users' data before the privacy-preserving data analysis [2]. However, such approaches may not be feasible or practical in scenarios where no trusted curator exists. Given this, Local Differential Privacy (LDP) [3] has been proposed to achieve differential privacy by letting the users add noises individually; however, LDP suffers from low utility due to the accumulated noise. To address this, the shuffle model of differential privacy (shuffle DP) [1,4,5] adds a shuffler between the users and the server, which randomly shuffles the noisy data before sending it to the server. Shuffle DP has an intriguing theoretical privacy amplification effect: a small amount of local noise can result in a strong privacy guarantee against the untrusted server. Extensive studies [4,5,6,7,8,9] have been devoted to proving a better (tighter) privacy amplification in shuffle DP.

However, most existing studies have focused on the shuffle model based on an (\epsilon_{0},\delta_{0}) -LDP randomizer with uniform and limited settings of the local privacy parameters \epsilon_{0} and \delta_{0}. For example, [5] assumes 0<\epsilon_{0}<1/2 and \delta_{0}=0. A recent work [10] provides a privacy bound for a local personalized privacy parameter \epsilon_{i} for each user i (and a fixed \delta_{0}), but the bound is relatively rough and has much room for improvement. To address this problem, we make the following contributions.

Firstly, we propose a Generalized Shuffle framework for Privacy Amplification (GSPA) that allows arbitrary local privacy parameters, and we provide a new privacy amplification analysis. Our analysis technique benefits from adopting Functional Differential Privacy [11] and from carefully analyzing the distance between two multinomial distributions (see Theorem 1 and 2). For both uniform and personalized privacy parameter settings, we provide lower privacy bounds that exceed those of existing results (see Figure 2).

Secondly, we apply GSPA with different personalized privacy parameter settings to diverse privacy-preserving analysis tasks, including private mean, private frequency estimation, and DP-SGD, to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. For mean and frequency estimation with GSPA (see Figure 3), the more conservative users there are, the less utility is observed, which shows a negative linear relationship. At the same time, as the privacy parameters of conservative users increase, utility shows a positive linear relationship. For DP-SGD with GSPA (see Figure 4), we observe an interesting phenomenon: although the constant scenario (\epsilon_{0}=0.5) offers stronger privacy protection, its test accuracy (94.8%) is higher than that (93.5%) of the U(0.01,2) scenarios, which have varying local privacy parameters.
